He goes to Gaul, which is in modern-day France, spending many years there. What he’s doing is trying to pacify the people of Gaul through a series of military campaigns that culminate in the battle of Alicia, one of the most famous battles in history. This is the very last battle of Caesar's Gallic campaign where he surrounds a village with his enemies inside.

The Romans build fortifications to block out the invaders, fighting on both fronts: against the enemies trapped inside and those converging from outside. The battle of Alicia is among the greatest in human history. 

Caesar has three main reasons for going to Gaul and starting these wars. First, slaves were the most valuable commodity at that time. He captures them by leading his soldiers into war, famously stating he killed a third of the people, enslaved a third, and left a third alone. He likely exaggerated the number killed to keep more money for himself.

Second, Caesar built a loyal private army by giving money to these soldiers, making them not only loyal but experienced in Gaul. This gave him the world’s most powerful army.

Third, he created a myth of himself as a great conqueror. He had people go back to Rome and announce his victories, though many were likely fabricated. This made him appear as an energetic, dynamic, and entrepreneurial military genius among the Romans.

The Roman Senate gets annoyed at Caesar for trying to become king of Rome, impeaching him and putting him on trial. Caesar rebels against them, starting a civil war where he aims to conquer the entire Roman Empire with just his army.
